t.1.10.1: Ruru said: My wife, dear to me as my own life, was bitten by a snake. Then, O serpent, I myself made a terrible vow.
t.1.10.3: The serpents that bite men here are others, O brahmin; you ought not to harm ḍuṇḍubhas merely because they smell like snakes.
t.1.10.2: "May I always slay every snake that I see," so indeed I resolved; therefore I seek to kill you, and you shall be released from your life.
t.1.10.5: Sūta said: Having heard these words of the serpent, Ruru, then stricken with fear, did not kill the ḍuṇḍubha, believing him to be a seer.
t.1.10.4: Knowing dharma as you do, you ought not to harm the ḍuṇḍubhas, who share the misfortunes of other snakes but not their aims, who share their sorrows but not their joys.
t.1.10.7: Formerly, O Ruru, I was a seer named Sahasrapād; through the curse of a brahmin I have come to the state of a serpent.
t.1.10.6: And the blessed Ruru, as if to calm him, said to him: "Tell me, if you will, O serpent, who are you that have come to this altered state?"
t.1.10.8: Ruru said: For what reason did the angry Brahmin curse you, O best of serpents? And for how long will this body of yours remain?
